name: Tongue scraping

card.summary: Daily scraping of the tongue's surface to remove coating, used to freshen breath and keep the tongue looking clean and pink.
card.note: Scraping too hard or too far back can cause gagging or irritation.

quick.overview:
Tongue scraping means drawing a scraper or brush across the top of the tongue to remove the coating of bacteria, food debris and dead cells. People use it as part of an oral hygiene routine to reduce a white or coloured tongue coating and to keep breath fresh, which supports a cleaner-looking mouth and more confident close contact.

The practice is traditional in Ayurveda and has been used in many cultures. Systematic reviews have examined its effect on breath odour and tongue coating, and their conclusions are cautious about how large the effect on halitosis is.
quick.how: A dedicated scraper (a metal or plastic strap, or a bristle tool) is typically pulled from the back of the tongue toward the tip and rinsed between strokes, usually as part of morning brushing. Some people use a toothbrush instead. It is commonly paired with brushing, flossing and mouthwash.
quick.risks: Pressing too hard or reaching too far back can cause gagging, irritation or small ulcers. A case report described possible infective endocarditis after tongue cleaner use, and people with high-risk heart valves are advised to ask a clinician.

lead: Tongue scraping, or tongue cleaning, is the removal of the coating on the tongue's upper surface using a scraper, brush or similar device.[1] The tongue's papillae trap microbes, food debris, saliva and dead cells, and cleaning it is done less often than brushing, flossing or rinsing.[1]

People do it for fresher breath and a cleaner-looking tongue; Wikipedia notes that reducing a white or coloured coating is mainly an aesthetic effect.[1] Researchers have also asked whether it reduces breath odour, and reviews report mixed or cautious results.[2][3]
The practice has roots in Ayurveda, where it is part of daily hygiene to remove a substance called ama.[1]

chain: Scraper removes the surface coating of the tongue
Less bacterial load and visible coating
Fresher breath and a cleaner, pinker tongue
angle.text: Scraping visibly reduces tongue coating, which changes how the tongue looks when speaking or smiling. Users also adopt it to lower mouth odour, which matters in close social contact.

paras: Scrapers come as plastic or metal straps, bristle rakes or circular handled devices, and ergonomic designs follow tongue anatomy.[1] Toothbrushes are also used, though Wikipedia notes they are narrower and designed for teeth rather than the tongue's spongy surface, and some have tongue-cleaning projections.[1]

Ayurveda recommends tongue cleaning daily, and traditional scrapers were made of copper, silver, gold, tin or brass.[1] Tongue hygiene has also been practised in Africa, Arabia, Europe, South America and many Eastern cultures; in Western societies between the 15th and 19th centuries it was mostly practised by the affluent, and commercial devices appeared in the 20th century.[1]

Cleaning can cause discomfort, and improper use may trigger the gag reflex or vomiting; aggressive scraping can cause irritation or ulcers.[1] One reported case involved possible infective endocarditis after tongue cleaner use, and people with prior endocarditis or high-risk valves may be more vulnerable to bacteria entering the bloodstream.[1]

A 2006 Cochrane review of tongue scraping for halitosis included two trials with 40 participants; the trials were methodologically sound but reported no data for the review's primary outcomes, and volatile sulfur compound levels were assessed as secondary outcomes.[4] That review was withdrawn in 2016 and replaced by a broader Cochrane review of halitosis interventions published in 2019, which incorporates the earlier tongue scraping and mouthrinse reviews.[2][3]

A 2010 systematic review in the International Journal of Dental Hygiene compared mechanical tongue cleaning with no tongue cleaning on breath odour and tongue coating.[5] Wikipedia summarises the research as not having reached clear conclusions about breath odour, while cleaning can reduce visible coating.[1]
